newsitem.title: USA: New fines proposed for controversial Maine egg farm.
newsitem.headline: New fines proposed for controversial Maine egg farm.

text.p: Federal officials Friday proposed an additional $117,000 in safety fines for a Maine egg farm that was denounced by former Labour Secretary Robert Reich as an "agricultural sweatshop."

Decoster Egg Farm workers were forced to make fly-paper without being told about the danger of the pesticide they were using or given protective equipment, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration charged in a complaint Friday.
"It is unfortunate that this employer continues to exhibit a fundamental disregard for the safety and health of its workers," OHSA'a regional administrator C. William Freeman said in a statement.
Officials at Decoster -- a privately owned company that is North America's largest producer of brown shell eggs -- declined immediate comment, saying they had not received a copy of OSHA's complaint.

Flypaper is a necessity on all farms and it can be purchased commercially, but Decoster manufactured it using masking tape and Golden Malrin pesticide. Inappropriate exposure to Golden Malrin pesticide can cause headaches, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhoea and pulmonary distress.
Safety officials last year proposed $3.6 million in fines for Decoster, citing serious health and safety violations in the working and housing conditions of its largely Hispanic workforce.

Last summer, then-U.S. Secretary of Labour Reich called Decoster an "agricultural sweatshop" and said the violations represented a "disregard also of the ways in which members of a civil society should treat one another as basic human beings."

Decoster denied wrongdoing and hired management consultants to address the government's concerns. The consultants -- including the head of the Maine Chamber of Commerce -- have since quite citing disagreements with the farm's owner.

Decoster is also in court in Iowa, where state officials have charged the company with environmental and safety violations at two hog farms. Decoster has accused Iowa of unfairly targeting it for punishment.

Several New England grocery store chains stopped or reduced their egg purchases from Decoster because of last year's labour complaints. The farm has offset those lost sales with increased exports to Asia, according to industry observers.
